t: Key events: Islamic Caliphates & Middle East
cards: The Sasanians, native speakers of Middle Persian, take power from the Parthian Arsacids, and Middle Persian becomes the prestige language of the state
Surena's Parthian army destroys the Roman army of Crassus at Carrhae
Mark Antony's invasion ends in a costly Roman retreat
Trajan captures the Parthian capital, Ctesiphon
Ardashir I kills Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan, founding the Sasanian Empire
An Assyrian inscription names “Gindibu the Arab” among the enemies of Shalmaneser III, the first known mention of Arabs
The Namara inscription, the epitaph of Imru' al-Qays, “king of all the Arabs”, is carved in Arabic in Nabataean letters
The Zabad inscription, in Greek, Syriac and Arabic, is one of the oldest dated texts in the Arabic script
Arabic becomes an official language of the United Nations
Alans cross the Rhine with the Vandals and Suebi
The Visigoths destroy the Alans of Hispania and kill their king Addac
Alans cross with the Vandals to North Africa
Alans under Sangiban fight Attila at the Catalaunian Plains
Ardashir I defeats and kills the last Parthian king, Artabanus IV, at Hormozdgan
Shapur I captures the Roman emperor Valerian at the Battle of Edessa
Shapur II wins Nisibis and lands beyond the Tigris in a peace with Rome's Jovian
Khosrow II's general Shahrbaraz captures Jerusalem
Heraclius defeats the Sasanians at the Battle of Nineveh
The last king, Yazdegerd III, is murdered near Merv
Nikoloz Cholokashvili’s Alphabetum Ibericum and Georgian–Italian dictionary, the first printed books partly in Georgian, appear for Catholic missionaries
Mesrop Mashtots creates the Armenian alphabet of 36 letters
Azdarar, the first Armenian periodical, is published in Classical Armenian
Heinrich Hübschmann uses the comparative method to show that Armenian is not an Iranian language
The Hijra: Muhammad and his followers migrate from Mecca to Medina, the start of the Islamic calendar
Muhammad dies in Medina; Abu Bakr becomes the first caliph
Husayn, Muhammad’s grandson, is killed at Karbala, an event central to Shia Islam
Muslim armies cross from North Africa into Spain
The Republic of Turkey abolishes the Ottoman caliphate
Abu Bakr is acclaimed first caliph after Muhammad's death and launches the Ridda Wars
Umar ibn al-Khattab succeeds Abu Bakr and accelerates the conquests
Khalid ibn al-Walid and Abu Ubayda defeat the Byzantines at the Yarmuk
Victory at Nihawand breaks the last organised Sasanian field army
Rebels assassinate Uthman, triggering the First Fitna
Ali and Muawiya fight the inconclusive Battle of Siffin
Ibn Muljam assassinates Ali at Kufa; the Umayyad Caliphate follows
Muawiyah secures the caliphate after Ali's assassination and rules from Damascus
Husayn ibn Ali is killed at Karbala, the defining martyrdom of Shia Islam
Tariq ibn Ziyad crosses into Spain and overthrows the Visigothic kingdom
The second Arab siege of Constantinople begins and fails the following year
Charles Martel checks Umayyad raids at the Battle of Tours
Abu Muslim proclaims the Abbasid Revolution in Khorasan
Marwan II is defeated at the Great Zab and killed, ending Umayyad rule in the east
Abbasid rebels defeat the Umayyads at the Battle of the Great Zab
Al-Mansur founds the Round City of Baghdad on the Tigris
Al-Mu'tasim moves the capital to Samarra to house his Turkic slave army
Assassination of al-Mutawakkil begins the Anarchy at Samarra
The Buyids take Baghdad, leaving the caliphs only religious authority
Hulagu Khan's Mongols sack Baghdad and execute Caliph al-Musta'sim
Selim I conquers Egypt, ending the Mamluk-sponsored shadow caliphate in Cairo
Haytham ibn Khalid declares himself Shirvanshah
Nizami completes Layla and Majnun for Akhsitan I
The Mongols under Jebe and Subutai take Shamakhi
Ibrahim I founds the Derbendi line and revives the state
Khalilullah I completes the mosque of his palace in Baku
Farrukh Yasar kills Shaykh Haydar, father of the future Shah Ismail
Ismail I defeats and kills Farrukh Yasar at the Battle of Jabani
Tahmasp I annexes Shirvan to the Safavid Empire
Ali ibn Buya takes Fars and makes Shiraz his base
Ahmad ibn Buya enters Baghdad and the brothers receive their titles
Public Ashura mourning and the feast of Ghadir are introduced in Baghdad
Adud al-Dawla defeats Bakhtiyar and unites the Buyid lands
Death of Adud al-Dawla, followed by rivalry among his sons
Tughril Beg enters Baghdad and ends Buyid rule in Iraq
The last Buyid prince in Fars is killed by Fadluya
Bagrat III unites western and eastern Georgia
David IV routs a Muslim coalition at the Battle of Didgori
David IV captures Tbilisi and makes it his capital
Georgian-backed Komnenos brothers found the Empire of Trebizond
Queen Rusudan submits to the Mongols
Timur takes Tbilisi and captures King Bagrat V
A royal council accepts the division of Georgia into separate kingdoms
Hamza ibn Ali begins to preach the Unitarian doctrine in Cairo, and the divine call is opened
The caliph al-Hakim has the preacher al-Darazi executed, leaving Hamza ibn Ali the sole leader of the new faith
After al-Hakim’s disappearance the regent Sitt al-Mulk orders the army to destroy the movement, opening years of persecution, the mihna
Baha al-Din al-Muqtana declares that no new pledges will be accepted, and the faith closes to converts
After a fatwa of Ibn Taymiyya, the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad inflicts a disastrous defeat on the Druze at Keserwan
The Ottoman sultan has Fakhr-al-Din II killed, the Ma’an emir under whom Druze dominion had reached from the Antioch plain to Safad
The battle of Ain Dara routs the Yamani faction, and many Yamani Druze migrate from Mount Lebanon to the Hauran
Tughril and Chaghri take Merv and Nishapur, throwing off Ghaznavid authority
Tughril and Chaghri rout the Ghaznavid sultan Masud I at Dandanaqan
Tughril enters Baghdad and is recognised as sultan by the Abbasid caliph
Alp Arslan defeats and captures the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV at Manzikert
Vizier Nizam al-Mulk is assassinated and Malik Shah dies weeks later, sparking civil war
The Qara Khitai defeat Sultan Sanjar at the Battle of Qatwan
Sanjar's death ends the eastern Seljuk line
The Khwarazm Shah Tekish kills Toghrul III, extinguishing the Great Seljuks
Ala ad-Din Tekish comes to power and throws off Seljuk overlordship
Tekish defeats and kills Toghrul III, the last Seljuk sultan of Iraq
Ala ad-Din Muhammad II takes the throne and expands against the Ghurids and Qara Khitai
Muhammad II's march on Baghdad is abandoned in the snows of the Zagros
Otrar's governor massacres a Mongol-sponsored caravan; the shah executes a Mongol envoy
Bukhara and Samarkand fall to Genghis Khan's armies
The empire effectively ceases to exist; Jalal ad-Din is defeated on the Indus
Jalal ad-Din dies after a decade of resistance in Iran and the Caucasus
The First Crusade takes Nicaea and defeats Kilij Arslan I at Dorylaeum
Kilij Arslan II defeats Manuel I Komnenos at Myriokephalon
Kaykhusraw I captures the port of Antalya
Kayqubad I takes Alanya and fortifies it
The Mongols crush the Seljuk army at the Battle of Köse Dağ
The poet and mystic Rumi dies in Konya
Ruben, a noble close to the murdered Bagratid king Gagik II, raises Armenian troops against the Byzantine Empire and founds the principality of Cilicia.
Prince Levon II is crowned King Levon I in the cathedral of Tarsus on 6 January, with a banner from Henry VI, Holy Roman Emperor; Cilician Armenia becomes a kingdom.
Queen Zabel is forced to marry Het'um, son of the regent Constantine of Baberon; as Het'um I he unites the rival Rubenid and Het'umid houses.
Het'um I visits Möngke Khan at Karakorum, confirming the Armeno-Mongol alliance his brother Smbat negotiated in 1247–1250.
Mamluk forces under Al-Mansur Ali and Qalawun overrun the Armenians at the Disaster of Mari, sack and burn Sis, massacre thousands and take 40,000 captives.
Het'um II joins the Mongol khan Ghazan to defeat the Mamluks at the Battle of Wadi al-Khazandar on 23 December.
The Mongol representative Bularghu murders King Levon III, the former king Het'um II and their party outside Anazarba; Oshin drives him out and becomes king.
Sis falls to the Mamluks, then the fortress of Gaban where King Levon V had taken refuge; the kingdom ends and Levon dies in exile in Paris in 1393.
Baldwin I is crowned the first king at Bethlehem
Tyre falls to the Franks and a Venetian fleet
Baldwin IV defeats Saladin at Montgisard
Saladin destroys the Frankish army at Hattin and takes Jerusalem
Frederick II regains Jerusalem by treaty
The Mamluks take Acre, ending the kingdom
Badr al-Din Lu’lu, ruler of Mosul, has Sheikh Hasan, the leader who had consolidated the Yazidi community, killed
A joint army of neighbouring Sunni Kurdish tribes ransacks Lalish
The Ottoman Sheikh al-Islam issues fatwas legitimising the killing of Yazidis and the enslavement and sale of Yazidi women
An Ottoman army under Melek Ahmed Pasha storms Mount Sinjar, where 3,060 Yazidis are killed
The forces of Muhammad Pasha of Rawanduz massacre the Yazidis of Sheikhan, enslave thousands and execute those who refuse Islam
During the Armenian genocide many Yazidis are killed, and others flee from Van, Kars and Bazîd to Transcaucasia
The Islamic State captures Sinjar and begins the genocide of the Yazidis: over 5,000 are killed and thousands of women and girls forced into sexual slavery
After the murder of Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi, the Seljuk Empire names Zengi, son of Aq Sunqur al-Hajib, atabeg of Mosul.
Zengi captures the County of Edessa from the Crusaders after the siege of Edessa, a feat that makes him a hero in the Muslim world.
Nur ad-Din captures Damascus from the Turkic Burid dynasty and rules Syria from there.
Shirkuh kills the vizier Shawar and seizes Egypt as Fatimid vizier in Nur ad-Din's name; on his death the same year his nephew Saladin succeeds him.
Nur ad-Din dies on 15 May; his eleven-year-old son as-Salih Ismail inherits, and Saladin enters Damascus on 23 November.
Imad ad-Din Zangi hands Aleppo to Saladin on 12 June in exchange for Sinjar, Nusaybin and Raqqa, ending Zengid rule in Syria.
Badr al-Din Lu'lu', atabeg to the child emirs of Mosul, takes the city in his own name, possibly after murdering the last Zengid emir Nasir ad-Din Mahmud.
Al-Jazira in northern Iraq, the last Zengid territory, falls to an-Nasir Yusuf, the Ayyubid emir of Aleppo.
Saladin ends the Fatimid Caliphate, restoring Egypt to Sunni Abbasid allegiance
After Nur al-Din's death, Saladin takes Damascus
Saladin destroys the Crusader army at Hattin and takes Jerusalem
Treaty of Jaffa ends the Third Crusade with Jerusalem still in Ayyubid hands
Saladin dies, triggering a succession struggle among his sons
Al-Kamil cedes Jerusalem to Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II
Bahri mamluks murder Sultan Turanshah and seize Egypt
Alexios and David Komnenos seize Trebizond with Georgian troops
The Seljuks take Sinop and capture Alexios I
Trebizond becomes a vassal of the Mongols
John II gives up the title of Emperor of the Romans
Alexios III begins a long reign that restores order
Emperor David surrenders Trebizond to Mehmed II
David and most of his family are executed in Constantinople
Qutb ud-Din Aibak founds the Mamluk or Slave Dynasty after Muhammad of Ghor's murder
Abbasid caliph sends Iltutmish a diploma recognising him as sultan
Alauddin Khalji's forces turn back a Mongol army that reaches Delhi's outskirts
Malik Kafur plunders the Pandya lands around Madurai
Muhammad bin Tughlaq forcibly moves the capital to Daulatabad
The Bahmani Sultanate breaks away in the Deccan
Timur sacks Delhi and carries off its artisans to Samarkand
Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat
Mamluks assassinate Turanshah, the last Ayyubid sultan of Egypt, and seize power
Qutuz and Baybars defeat the Mongols at Ain Jalut; Baybars then takes the throne
Al-Ashraf Khalil captures Acre, ending the Crusader states
Al-Nasir Muhammad orders the rawk, a new land survey that reshapes the iqta system
The Black Death reaches Egypt, beginning repeated catastrophic population losses
Barquq inaugurates the Burji regime of Circassian mamluks
The Portuguese defeat a Mamluk fleet at Diu, cutting customs revenue
Selim I wins at Ridaniya and conquers Egypt, ending Mamluk sovereignty
Hulagu destroys the Nizari Ismaili state and takes Alamut
Mongol forces capture Baghdad and execute the Abbasid caliph al-Mustasim
The Mamluks defeat Kitbuqa's Mongol army at Ain Jalut in Galilee
The monk Rabban Sauma begins an embassy to Europe seeking an alliance against the Mamluks
Ghazan converts to Islam and begins sweeping reforms with Rashid al-Din
Ghazan wins at Wadi al-Khaznadar, briefly taking Damascus
Rashid al-Din, the state's ablest administrator, is executed
Abu Said dies without an heir and the Ilkhanate fragments
David VI Narin withdraws to Kutaisi and founds a western kingdom
George V the Brilliant reunites Imereti with the rest of Georgia
Bagrat of Imereti defeats George VIII at Chikhori
The division of Georgia leaves Imereti a separate kingdom
The Treaty of Amasya places western Georgia in the Ottoman sphere
Solomon I defeats the Ottomans at Chikhori
Solomon II accepts Russian protection by the Treaty of Elaznauri
Russia deposes Solomon II and annexes Imereti
Osman I defeats a Byzantine force at the Battle of Bapheus
Orhan captures Bursa, the dynasty's first true capital
Mehmed II captures Constantinople after a siege of some fifty-three days
Suleiman the Magnificent destroys the Hungarian royal army at Mohács
Jan III Sobieski routs the Ottoman army at the second siege of Vienna
The Tanzimat reforms begin to modernise administration and law
The Grand National Assembly abolishes the sultanate
Atatürk’s reforms replace the Perso-Arabic script with an extended Latin alphabet and begin replacing Arabic and Persian loanwords
Turkey’s Education Council decides that Ottoman Turkish should be taught in Islamic high schools and as an elective in other schools
Qara Mahammad invades Mardin and takes the submission of its Artuqid ruler Majd al-Din Isa, who becomes a vassal.
Timur defeats the Qara Qoyunlu; Qara Yusuf flees to the Mamluk Sultanate, where an-Nasir Faraj imprisons him together with the Jalayirid sultan Ahmad.
Qara Yusuf crushes the Timurids Abu Bakr and Miran Shah at the Battle of Sardrud on 20 April; Miran Shah is killed.
Qara Yusuf conquers Tabriz, executes Shaykh Uways Jalayir, captures Baghdad and takes control of Armenia; the Qara Qoyunlu are independent.
Qara Yusuf dies in December; his sons fight for the succession and Shah Rukh invades, occupying Tabriz briefly in 1421.
On Shah Rukh's death Jahan Shah throws off Timurid vassalage, takes the titles sultan and khan and seizes Sultaniya, Hamadan and Qazvin.
Jahan Shah advances to Herat and holds the Timurid capital for some months, until Hasan Ali's revolt and Abu Said's march on Tabriz force him back.
Jahan Shah is killed at the Battle of Chapakchur after his failed attack on Aq Qoyunlu Diyarbakır; by 1468 Uzun Hasan has conquered Iraq, Azerbaijan and western Iran.
Qara Yuluk Osman defeats and kills Kadi Burhan al-Din
Uzun Hasan defeats and kills the Qara Qoyunlu ruler Jahan Shah
Uzun Hasan defeats the Timurid Abu Sa’id and makes Tabriz his capital
Mehmed II defeats Uzun Hasan at the Battle of Otlukbeli
Death of Ya’qub opens a decade of succession wars
Ismail defeats Alvand at Sharur and takes Tabriz
Ismail defeats Murad near Hamadan, ending Aq Qoyunlu rule
Ivan the Terrible marries Maria Temryukovna, daughter of the Kabardian prince Temryuk
Kabardians defeat a Crimean army at the Battle of Kanzhal
Russia founds Mozdok, beginning its advance into Kabarda
Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca recognises Kabarda as Russian
Ottomans cede the Circassian coast to Russia in the Treaty of Adrianople
Circassian delegates meet in a united assembly at Sochi
Russia ends Circassian resistance; mass deportation to the Ottoman Empire
Ismail I defeats the Aq Qoyunlu, seizes Tabriz and proclaims Twelver Shiism the state religion
Selim I's Ottoman guns and janissaries rout the Qizilbash cavalry at Chaldiran
Shah Abbas I's reformed army recovers Herat and Khorasan from the Uzbeks
Abbas I begins moving the Armenian merchants of Julfa to New Julfa beside Isfahan
Abbas I expels the Portuguese from Hormuz with English naval help
The Treaty of Zuhab fixes a Safavid-Ottoman frontier close to today's Iran-Iraq border
Mir Mahmud Hotak wins at Gulnabad and takes Isfahan after a seven-month siege
Nader Quli Afshar is proclaimed Shah on the Mughan plain, ending the Safavid dynasty
Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat and founds the empire
Babur defeats the Rajput confederacy of Rana Sanga at Khanwa
Humayun recovers Delhi after years of exile under Sher Shah Suri's rule
Akbar begins his reign, turning a fragile conquest into a stable empire
Akbar abolishes the jizya tax on non-Muslims
Aurangzeb annexes Golconda, bringing the empire near its greatest extent
Nader Shah of Persia sacks Delhi and carries off the Peacock Throne
The British exile Bahadur Shah II, the last emperor, to Rangoon
Qawasim traditionally said to establish their rule at Sharjah
British expedition destroys Qasimi naval power; Sharjah becomes the family’s main seat
Sultan bin Saqr signs the General Maritime Treaty with Britain
Perpetual Maritime Truce ends warfare at sea
Exclusive Agreement places foreign relations under Britain
Imperial Airways opens a rest house and airfield at Sharjah
Britain deposes Sheikh Saqr bin Sultan
Sharjah joins the United Arab Emirates on 2 December
Nader expels the Ghilzai Afghans from Isfahan after seven years of occupation
Nader is proclaimed Shah after a great assembly on the Mughan plain
Nader crushes a much larger Mughal army at Karnal and enters Delhi
Nader campaigns in Central Asia, subduing Bukhara and Khiva
Nader has his eldest son Reza Qoli blinded on suspicion of plotting
Nader defeats the Ottomans at Kars
Nader Shah is assassinated by his own officers near Quchan
Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar takes Mashhad; Shahrokh dies, ending the dynasty
Nader Shah's assassination leaves Iran in a power vacuum
Karim Khan lets the British East India Company open a factory at Bushehr
Karim Khan restores the tomb of the poet Hafez in Shiraz
Sadeq Khan's forces capture Basra from the Ottomans after a long siege
Karim Khan dies, opening fifteen years of Zand civil war
Shiraz's governor betrays the city to the Qajars
Agha Mohammad Khan takes Kerman and executes the last Zand ruler, Lotf Ali Khan
Agha Mohammad Khan makes Tehran his capital
Agha Mohammad Khan is crowned shah
Treaty of Gulistan cedes Georgia and most of the Caucasian khanates to Russia
Treaty of Turkmenchay surrenders Erivan and Nakhichevan
Amir Kabir founds the Dar ol-Fonun in Tehran
The Majlis deposes Ahmad Shah, ending the dynasty
Muhammad Ali founds a government press at Bulaq, near Cairo, which prints its first book in 1822
Rifa’a al-Tahtawi goes to Paris as imam of an Egyptian student mission; his account of France appears in 1834
Marun al-Naqqash stages al-Bakhil in Beirut, the first play in Arabic
Butrus al-Bustani founds the National School in Beirut, open to pupils of every religion
The newspaper al-Ahram begins publication in Alexandria and the journal al-Muqtataf in Beirut
Jurji Zaydan founds al-Hilal in Cairo; Hind Nawfal launches al-Fatat, the first Arabic magazine for women
Muhammad Abduh becomes Grand Mufti of Egypt; Qasim Amin publishes The Liberation of Women
The Ottoman constitution is restored, loosening censorship, and the Egyptian University opens in Cairo
The Báb declares his mission in Shiraz
The Báb is executed by a firing squad in Tabriz
Bahá’u’lláh declares his mission in the Garden of Ridván in Baghdad
Bahá’u’lláh is exiled to the Ottoman prison city of Acre
Bahá’u’lláh dies near Acre; his son ʻAbdu’l-Bahá leads the faith
ʻAbdu’l-Bahá travels across North America, speaking in churches, synagogues and universities
The Universal House of Justice, the faith’s governing body, is elected for the first time
A British civilian administration under High Commissioner Sir Herbert Samuel replaces military rule in July; riots in Jerusalem in April have killed five Jews and four Arabs.
The League of Nations grants Britain the Mandate for Palestine; the Palestine Order in Council plans a Legislative Council whose seats the Arabs reject, boycotting the 1923 elections.
Riots in August, including the Hebron massacre of Jews, leave 250 people dead.
The Arab general strike of April to October, led by the Arab Higher Committee under Amin al-Husseini, opens the Arab revolt in Palestine.
The revolt ends in March with more than 5,000 Arabs, 400 Jews and 200 British dead; the White Paper restricts Jewish immigration and land purchase and promises an independent state within ten years.
The Irgun blows up the King David Hotel in Jerusalem, headquarters of the British administration, killing 92 people; Britain begins interning illegal Jewish immigrants in Cyprus.
The UN General Assembly adopts Resolution 181 on 29 November, recommending partition into Arab and Jewish states; civil war between the two communities begins at once.
The Mandate expires at midnight on 14–15 May; David Ben-Gurion declares the State of Israel, Arab armies cross the borders, and the 1948 war divides the territory.
The Republic is proclaimed in Ankara after the Treaty of Lausanne and the withdrawal of the last Allied troops from Istanbul on 4 October; Mustafa Kemal becomes its first president.
Women gain the right to vote nationally; the Surname Law gives Mustafa Kemal the name Atatürk.
Atatürk dies and İsmet İnönü becomes the second president; Turkey stays neutral in almost all of the Second World War.
After fighting with the UN forces in the Korean War, Turkey joins NATO as a bulwark against Soviet expansion into the Mediterranean.
The third military coup, after those of 1960 and 1971; the constitution still in force is approved by referendum in 1982.
Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's Justice and Development Party (AKP) wins power, beginning more than two decades of AKP government.
On 15 July an attempted coup fails; by 2024 the government counts 13,251 people jailed in connection with it.
A referendum replaces the parliamentary republic with an executive presidency and abolishes the office of prime minister.
On 1 September the Lebanese Republic is proclaimed under the French Mandate, with a constitution inspired by France's adopted on 23 May; the country stays under French control.
The new government abolishes the mandate on 8 November and is imprisoned by the French; under British pressure the officials are released on 22 November and France accepts Lebanon's independence.
Full-scale civil war breaks out between Christian groups and the forces of the PLO and left-wing Druze and Muslim militias.
Parliament agrees the Taif Agreement, with a timetable for Syrian withdrawal and equal Christian and Muslim representation; the war ends at the end of 1990.
Israeli forces withdraw fully from southern Lebanon in May; 25 May becomes Liberation Day.
Former Prime Minister Rafic Hariri is assassinated on 14 February; mass demonstrations force Syria to withdraw its troops by 26 April.
Mass protests from 17 October against sectarian rule, corruption and the liquidity crisis; the currency collapses and the state defaults in 2020.
Israel invades on 1 October after killing Hezbollah's leader Hassan Nasrallah on 27 September; a ceasefire follows in November.
On 23 September Prince Faisal declares on Ibn Saud's behalf the unification of the kingdoms of Hejaz and Nejd as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, now the Saudi National Day.
Vast oil reserves are discovered in Al-Ahsa on the Persian Gulf; full-scale development begins in 1941 under the American-controlled Aramco.
Saudi Arabia leads an oil embargo against the Western countries that supported Israel in the Yom Kippur War, and oil prices quadruple.

The Iranian Revolution and the seizure of the Grand Mosque in Mecca by Islamist militants, retaken after ten days, push the royal family towards stricter religious observance and a greater role for the ulema.
After Iraq invades Kuwait, King Fahd asks the United States to intervene and allows American and coalition troops to be stationed in the kingdom; Saudi forces join the Gulf War of 1991.
King Fahd introduces the Basic Law in March; the Consultative Council of sixty appointed members is inaugurated in December 1993.
Saudi Arabia mobilises 150,000 troops and 100 fighter jets to intervene in the civil war in Yemen; women vote and stand in municipal elections for the first time.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman takes power; as many as 500 princes, ministers and businessmen are arrested in an anti-corruption campaign in November.
On 28 September a coup takes Syria out of the United Arab Republic and ends the political union with Egypt.
On 8 March the Military Committee of the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party seizes power and establishes a one-party state under martial law.
In the Six-Day War Israel captures two-thirds of the Golan Heights in under 48 hours.
Hafez al-Assad, Minister of Defense, deposes Salah Jadid in the bloodless Corrective Movement and becomes the state's strongman.
The Islamist uprising of the Muslim Brotherhood ends in the Hama massacre, in which Ba'athist troops and paramilitaries kill between 2,000 and 40,000 people.
Hafez al-Assad dies on 10 June; his son Bashar is elected president unopposed, and the Damascus Spring is suppressed by autumn 2001.
Protests from 26 January become a nationwide uprising; the army is sent against the cities and defectors form the Free Syrian Army.
On 8 December opposition forces led by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham capture Damascus, ending 53 years of Assad family rule; Bashar al-Assad flees to Moscow.
The NLF begins its armed uprising in the Radfan mountains
Britain withdraws and the People’s Republic of South Yemen is proclaimed on 30 November
The Corrective Move removes President Qahtan al-Shaabi
The country is renamed the People’s Democratic Republic of Yemen
The Yemeni Socialist Party is founded
Border war with North Yemen; treaty of friendship with the Soviet Union
Party civil war in Aden kills thousands, including Abdul Fattah Ismail
Unification with North Yemen forms the Republic of Yemen on 22 May
Zayed and Rashid agree to form a union after Britain announces its withdrawal from the Gulf
Six sheikhdoms proclaim the United Arab Emirates on 2 December
Ras al-Khaimah joins as the seventh emirate
Jebel Ali port opens; Rashid of Dubai becomes prime minister
The Gulf Cooperation Council is founded in Abu Dhabi
Zayed dies and is succeeded by Khalifa bin Zayed
Abu Dhabi rescues Dubai during the Dubai World debt crisis
The UAE signs the Abraham Accords with Israel
North and South Yemen unite as the Republic of Yemen on 22 May
Northern forces defeat a southern secession and take Aden
Treaty of Jeddah fixes the Saudi border; al-Qaeda bombs the USS Cole in Aden
The first of six wars against the Houthi movement begins in Saada
Mass protests force Saleh to agree to hand over power
A Saudi-led coalition intervenes in the war
A Presidential Leadership Council takes over the recognised government
Armenia declares its statehood on 21 September after the failed August coup in Moscow; Levon Ter-Petrosyan is elected the first president in October.
Turkey joins Azerbaijan's railway and air blockade of Armenia; the new currency, the dram, is introduced and suffers hyperinflation.
A Russian-brokered ceasefire ends the First Nagorno-Karabakh War, with some 30,000 dead and over a million displaced.
Armenia and Turkey sign protocols on 10 October to normalise relations and reopen their border, but they are never ratified.
Protests from April to May, the 'velvet revolution', force Serzh Sargsyan's resignation; parliament elects Nikol Pashinyan prime minister in May.
On 27 September Full-scale war erupts over Nagorno-Karabakh; the ceasefire after six weeks is seen by many as Armenia's defeat and capitulation.
Azerbaijan's offensive of 19–20 September ends the Republic of Artsakh, and almost its entire Armenian population flees to Armenia.
Parliament approves a bill endorsing EU accession on 12 February; on 8 August Pashinyan and Ilham Aliyev sign a joint declaration committing to a peace deal.
The Supreme Council of Azerbaijan adopts a Declaration of Independence on 18 October, affirmed by a nationwide referendum in December.
President Abulfaz Elchibey is overthrown by a military insurrection led by Colonel Surat Huseynov, which brings Heydar Aliyev to power.
The First Nagorno-Karabakh War ends with Armenians holding 14–16 percent of Azerbaijani territory; in September SOCAR signs a 30-year contract with 13 oil companies.
The constitution is adopted on 12 November, completing the formation of the political system.
Ilham Aliyev succeeds his father Heydar as President and chairman of the New Azerbaijan Party.
The Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline becomes operational in May, carrying Caspian oil to Turkey and world markets; the new manat is launched on 1 January.
The Second Nagorno-Karabakh War, six weeks from 27 September, ends in a ceasefire that returns the seven districts and parts of Nagorno-Karabakh to Azerbaijani control.
An offensive in September ends the Republic of Artsakh, dissolved on 1 January 2024, and nearly all ethnic Armenians are expelled from Nagorno-Karabakh.
The Supreme Council declares independence on 9 April after the referendum of 31 March; Zviad Gamsakhurdia is elected president on 26 May with 86.5 percent.
The civil war that began with the coup against Gamsakhurdia ends in December; Abkhaz separatists and North Caucasian militants expel some 230,000 to 250,000 Georgians from Abkhazia.
A new constitution is adopted and Eduard Shevardnadze, head of state since 1992, is elected president.
The Rose Revolution led by Mikheil Saakashvili, Zurab Zhvania and Nino Burjanadze deposes Shevardnadze after the fraudulent elections of 2 November.
Russia invades on 8 August after fighting in South Ossetia; a ceasefire follows on 12 August, and on 26 August Russia recognises Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent.
Georgian Dream defeats Saakashvili's United National Movement in the first peaceful electoral transfer of power, as the state becomes a parliamentary republic.
The European Council grants Georgia candidate status for EU membership in December, despite unfulfilled conditions.
The disputed election of 26 October and the suspension of EU accession until 2028 plunge the country into crisis; the outgoing president Salome Zourabichvili refuses to recognise her successor.
